opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing I'd say is that "full automation" is probably going to arrive much more gradually and unevenly than people imagine. In robotics especially, we tend to see a capability work in a lab demo and then assume it'll be everywhere a year later. In practice there's this long tail: getting a robot to fold laundry in one home is very different from getting it to work reliably in millions of homes, with all the weird edge cases. So I think society actually has more time to adapt than the most dramatic narratives suggest, and the planning question is less about one big moment and more about managing a long transition well.

The second thing is that I'm somewhat wary of trying to plan the end state in too much detail. Technologists have a pretty bad track record of predicting exactly which jobs go away and which ones appear. If you'd asked people in 1900 to plan for the automation of agriculture, they probably wouldn't have imagined the economy we ended up with. So I'd favor building institutions that are flexible and responsive: strong safety nets, easier ways for people to retrain or move between kinds of work, and policies that let the gains from productivity get broadly shared rather than concentrated.

That last point I think matters a lot. If automation really does make labor dramatically cheaper, the economic pie gets much bigger, and in principle everyone could be better off. Whether that actually happens is a political and social question, not a technical one. As researchers we can make the technology work, but how the benefits are distributed is something society has to decide deliberately.

And finally, I'd say a lot of the near-term value of automation is in doing things we currently just don't do enough of, because it's too expensive or too dangerous: elder care, cleaning up hazardous environments, building housing, scientific experimentation. If we frame it as "what would we do if physical labor were abundant" rather than only "whose job gets replaced," I think it opens up a more optimistic and also more useful way of planning for it.

r001.rationale: The response says planning should focus on managing the long transition and cautions against planning the end state in detail, clearly emphasizing the transition alongside the automated future.

r002.rationale: It names near-term uses such as elder care and hazardous cleanup, but does not say automation may first emerge in sectors people do not expect.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a big question, and I want to be careful here because my expertise is really in building the systems, not in economic policy. But I do think about this a lot, partly because the robotics side of things is where a lot of the physical-world automation would actually come from, so I feel some responsibility to at least have a view.

The first thing I'd say is that I don't think "full automation" arrives as a single event. It's going to be very uneven. On the digital side, you can already see software and knowledge work being transformed pretty rapidly. On the physical side, robotics lags, and the reason is basically data. Language models got to ride on this enormous corpus of human text that already existed. For robots, there's no internet of robot experience. You have to go out and collect it, and that means the capability curve is gated by deployment. You deploy robots that are kind of okay at something, they generate data, you train better models, you deploy more. It's a flywheel, but the flywheel has to be spun up, and that takes real time, real capital, real engineering.

So one implication for planning is that the timeline matters a lot, and it's not the same across sectors. If you plan as though everything gets automated in two years, you'll do things that are counterproductive. If you plan as though nothing happens for fifty years, you'll get caught flat-footed. I think the honest answer is that the physical world will be automated over a period of maybe a decade or two once the flywheel really gets going, and that's actually a window where society can adapt, if it chooses to.

The second thing is that I think people underestimate how much the way we deploy these systems is a choice. There's a version of automation where the technology is used to augment people, where a nurse or an electrician or a warehouse worker has a system that takes the tedious parts and leaves them doing more valuable things, and there's a version where it's used purely for replacement. Both are technically feasible with roughly the same models. The difference is economic incentives and institutional decisions, and those are things society actually can shape with policy, with how labor is organized, with how the benefits get distributed.

And the third thing, and this is more of a personal view, is that if this goes the way I think it might, the fundamental scarcity shifts. For most of history the bottleneck has been labor, both cognitive and physical. If that bottleneck goes away, then the question of what people do and how they derive meaning and income becomes the central question, not a side issue. I don't think the answer is just redistribution, although some of that will probably be necessary. I think we need to be deliberate about preserving human agency, about making sure the systems are things people can direct and understand rather than things that just happen to them.

I'm optimistic in the long run. Robots that can do dangerous, dirty, repetitive work are an enormous good. But I'm also aware that the transition is where the pain is, and that the people building the technology, myself included, don't get to just hand that problem off to someone else.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the transition is where the pain is and that society can adapt, but does not argue that planning should give the transition as much attention as the fully automated end state.

r002.rationale: The candidate contrasts rapid change in digital work with slower robotics, but does not suggest automation may first appear in sectors people do not expect.

astra-6.text:
I think we should plan for it, but we should be careful about assuming that we know exactly what full automation will look like. There’s a difference between a system being capable of doing a task and that task actually being automated throughout the economy. Deployment takes time, institutions take time to change, and those transitions can be quite painful even if the eventual outcome is very positive.

To me, the central question is how broadly the benefits are distributed. If we can produce everything people need with much less human labor, that’s an enormous opportunity. But our current mechanism for distributing purchasing power is largely employment. So we need to think about what happens when those two things become less tightly connected. Income support might be part of that, but so might broader ownership of the productive technology. I wouldn’t claim to know which policy is best.

I’d favor experimenting with those mechanisms early, while we still have time to learn. And I would separate the question of how people support themselves from the question of what gives their lives meaning. People pursue all kinds of difficult, meaningful activities without being paid for them. The challenge is making sure that the freedom to do that is available broadly.

r001.rationale: The response notes that deployment takes time and transitions can be painful, and favors early experimentation. It does not say the transition deserves as much attention as the fully automated end state.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest automation may first appear in sectors people do not expect.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should take that possibility seriously, but we should also be humble about how well we can predict what it looks like. There’s a big difference between automating most of the tasks people do today and having a society in which people have no useful role. I don’t think we know that the second follows from the first.

But there’s a real distribution question. If machines can produce much more of what everybody needs, that’s an enormous opportunity. It doesn’t automatically mean everybody benefits. If your access to those goods depends on selling your labor, and your labor is no longer in demand, then greater productive capacity alone doesn’t solve your problem. We need to think about how people share in that prosperity, whether through ownership, public services, income support, or some combination.

I would approach this as an adaptive process. Put institutions in place that can respond as we see what actually happens, and make sure people can weather the transition. You don’t want to require someone to correctly predict the next twenty years of technological development in order to have a decent life.

And then there’s the question of purpose. Work provides more than income: it provides community, structure, a sense that you contribute. Giving people material security is very important, but it doesn’t answer all of those questions. Ideally, automation gives people more freedom to pursue things they care about. Building a society where that freedom is meaningful seems like the thing to aim for.

r001.rationale: The response discusses adapting institutions and helping people through the transition, but it does not argue that the transition deserves as much attention as the fully automated end state.

r002.rationale: The response does not suggest that automation may first appear in sectors other than people expect.
